newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Hung parliament feared by Irish markets - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hung parliament feared by Irish markets - analysts.

text.p: The result most feared by the markets in Ireland's general election on Friday is a hung parliament in which neither of the country's two main political blocs wins overall control of parliament, analysts and traders say.

Opinion polls suggest the centre-right alliance of Fianna Fail and the Progresive Democrats will win more seats than the ruling centre-left "rainbow coalition" of Fine Gael, Labour and Democratic Left, but neither group may muster enough seats for a parliamentary majority.

An IMS poll for the Sunday Independent newspaper put support for Fianna Fail at 40 percent and the Progressive Democrats at six percent. The combined support for the three rainbow coalition parties was 42 percent. Ireland's system of proportional representation produces rough proportionality between votes cast for parties and seats won by them.

The paper said the poll "confirms that an inconclusive general election outcome is the most likely result", and that in such a scenario the support of the Green Party and independent members of parliament would be crucial.
But economists say this outcome would be the worst for the markets.
"What the market really does not want to see is a hung parliament. That is the greatest negative," Riada economist Padhraic Garvey told Reuters.

"The possible results of the election are not fully priced into the market yet. Looking at the polls up to now, a hung parliament is a real possibility, and that would be the worst scenario for us," one bond dealer said.
Analysts said pre-election uncertainty could keep Irish markets subdued this week.

"It is quite conceivable that the market will underperform over the entire election campaign," Garvey said. "Overseas investors know there is an election going on and elections breed uncertainty because people are not quite sure what the make-up of the new administration is going to be."
Economists say there is little to choose between the economic policies of the two main competing blocs.

The "rainbow coalition" can boast a record of high economic growth and low inflation, but some economists say it is too soft on public finances and too eager to enter economic and monetary union (EMU) whether or not Britain joins.
The Fianna Fail/Progressive Democratics alliance is seen as most likely to get tough on fiscal and monetary policy.

"The markets would prefer to see a Fianna Fail/ Progressive Democrat win, largely because the PDs would be seen as the party that would be tougher on public spending and fiscal policy, which is positive for the bond market," a bond dealer said.

Both of the main coalitions favour joining a single currency but Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats have sounded a more cautious note about joining EMU if Britain stays out. Several Irish economists have warned that joining EMU without Britain could be dangerous for Ireland's economy.
"The foreign exchange markets would obviously sit up and take notice if there was a Fianna Fail/PD coalition, especially if they brought the EMU issue to the fore," a currency trader said.
Equity dealers said if the opposition coalition gets elected it may spur privatisation of state bodies, which would broaden the scope and dimension of Irish equities.

PD leader Mary Harney advocates selling state assets and slashing 25,000 jobs in the public service, while the presence of left-wing parties in the government has constrained the sale of majority stakes in state-owned companies during the life of the current government, economists say.

"It is possible you could see a push to get Aer Rianta or Aer Lingus and one or two other state bodies into private hands under a Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government," one equity dealer said. "It would give a new dimension to the market, broadening scope for trade which would be positive for the bourse."
